title: Why Your Leads Are Not Converting (It Is Rarely the Ads)
metaTitle: Why Your Leads Are Not Converting
description: The six places an enquiry dies between the ad and the sale, in the order worth checking, starting with the one that is free to fix and usually the answer.

blocks.v: The campaign is delivering, the enquiries are arriving, and almost none of them turn into customers. The instinct is to blame the ads and change the targeting. The ads are usually not the problem.
Six places an enquiry dies, in the order worth checking. The first is free to fix and it is the answer more often than the other five combined.
1. Nobody answered fast enough
Check how long your average enquiry waits for a first response. Not your target, the actual figure from the last twenty.

In this market somebody enquiring about a service has usually enquired with two or three suppliers in the same ten minutes. The one who replies first is not just ahead, they are often the only one in the conversation. A reply that arrives the next working day arrives after the decision.
This costs nothing to fix and it is the most common answer. Before you change a single thing about the marketing, find out how long people are waiting.
2. The enquiry went somewhere nobody looks

Form submissions going to an address that forwards to someone who left. WhatsApp messages landing on a phone nobody checks at the weekend. A CRM integration that broke silently three months ago and nobody noticed because the absence of leads looks the same as a quiet month.
Test it yourself. Send a real enquiry through every route on your site, today, and see where it lands and how long it takes. It is a twenty-minute job and it finds something surprisingly often.
3. The ad promised something the page does not

The ad says one thing and the landing page says another, usually because they were made by different people at different times. The visitor arrives, fails to find what brought them in three seconds, and leaves.

This shows up as a good click-through rate and a terrible conversion rate, which is why the two numbers are only useful together. Read your ad and your page one after the other and ask whether the second obviously delivers on the first.
4. You are attracting the wrong people successfully
Everything is working and the people arriving cannot buy. Usually because the targeting optimised towards whoever was cheapest to reach, or because the offer never qualified anyone out.
The fix is uncomfortable: qualify harder and earlier. Put the price range on the page. Say who it is not for. Volume goes down and the qualified share goes up, which is the number that matters.
5. The form is doing the sales team's job badly

Every field costs you completions, and most forms collect three things nobody ever reads. A seven-field form filters people out, which sounds like qualification and is actually attrition: the serious buyer in a hurry abandons it alongside everyone else.
Name and a way to reach them. A sales person qualifies in ninety seconds what a form half-establishes in seven fields.
6. There is no follow-up at all
Somebody enquires, gets one reply, does not answer, and that is the end of it. Most businesses have no second touch and no third, which means every enquiry that was merely busy that week is lost.

Three follow-ups over two weeks, written as though a person sent them, recovers more revenue than almost any change you could make to the campaign. It is also the cheapest thing on this list after answering the phone.
The order matters

Work down the list rather than starting where it is most interesting. People tend to begin at three or four, because changing an ad feels like doing marketing and checking a response time feels like admin.
The first two are free, take an afternoon, and are the answer more often than the rest put together.
Frequently asked questions
How fast is fast enough to reply?

Minutes rather than hours, for anything where the person is actively comparing suppliers. If that is not possible, an automated first reply that genuinely helps, rather than one that says we will be in touch, holds the conversation open until somebody can.
Should I use a chatbot?

For routing and for an instant first response, yes. For pretending to be a person, no. A bot that answers the common question and hands over cleanly is useful. One that loops somebody through five menus to avoid staffing an inbox costs you the enquiry and the goodwill.
Is it the ads or the website?

Look at where people stop. High clicks and low form starts points at the page. High form starts and low completions points at the form. Plenty of enquiries and few customers points at response time or at who you are attracting, not at the campaign.
How many follow-ups is too many?

Three over two weeks is comfortable for most business audiences here, each one shorter than the last and each giving an easy way to say no. Beyond that you are trading goodwill for a small number of replies.
Published 6 October 2026 by a Dubai-based freelance digital marketer.
